paper_title: Polytropos: What Do Vision-Language Model Descriptions Make of a Cultural Object?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language models have become a new kind of describer, writing about almost anything people see, and their descriptions now shape how cultures are known by people and by other models. Descriptions of cultures tend to turn particular things into types, and what a description loses shows what its describer lacks. We introduce Polytropos, a benchmark that measures what model descriptions of cultural objects keep of the particular object by turning each description back into an image and comparing it with the original photograph. On 374 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty, with 1,870 descriptions from five models and 230 written by curators, reconstructions are recognised as the recorded culture more often than the photographs, at 54.55% to 59.09% against 52.14%, yet 16% to 21% of objects change outcome and only 0.49% of reconstructions are identified as the specific object. On the same objects, models lose recorded cultures at a rate similar to curators but gain more. Model descriptions give each object many faces, each typical of its culture and almost none the object itself.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Vision-language models have become new kind of describer, writing about almost anything people see, including the objects of every cultural tradition [14, 48, 55]. Their descriptions already enter catalogues, search results, and the training data of the next models [12, 46, 51], and through them shape how present and future generations know cultures they will never see. Descriptions of cultures have long turned particular things into types [1, 18]. describer does so where it knows thing less well than its kind and fills the gap with the kind [10, 28], which makes what description loses measure of what its describer does not know [15], measure recognition cannot give, since knowing the kind suffices to name culture. Do the descriptions of vision-language models keep the particular object, or only its kind? 1 Figure 1: Culture recovery differs despite language eligibility. A: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite; B: LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-8B. Images come from full unchanged descriptions; quotations are verbatim. We propose Polytropos, the first benchmark that measures what model descriptions of cultural objects keep of the particular object  (Table 1)  . fluent description that names the right culture reads as accurate, even to careful reader, so we turn each description back into an image and set it beside the original photograph, where what was kept, lost, or added becomes visible (Figure 1). The dataset contains 374 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty, stratified by region and object type, with 1,870 descriptions from five vision-language models, selected from fifteen because their descriptions are well formed for more than 90% of objects, and 230 museum-authored descriptions of the same objects as human baseline. The task renders each unchanged description with fixed text-to-image generator, and an image-only recogniser, which sees neither the description nor the source photograph, predicts the culture of the reconstruction (Figure 2). For evaluation, the same recogniser applied to the original photograph gives paired reference, so each object keeps, loses, or gains its recorded culture under each description, model and museum descriptions are compared on the same objects, and an identification probe tests whether the particular object can still be recognised. Across five models, reconstructions are recognised as the recorded culture more often than the photographs, at 54.55% to 59.09% against 52.14%, yet 16% to 21% of objects change outcome, and only 0.49% of reconstructions are identified as the specific object, against 2.67% of photographs. On the 230 objects that also have museum descriptions, models lose similar share of recorded cultures to curators, 9.13% to 11.74% against 11.74%, but gain more, 10.87% to 15.22% against 10.87%, moving objects toward what their culture typically looks like. Museum text also points to particular object in 32.61% of descriptions, against 7.83% to 13.04% for model text. The descriptions show how. They frame objects in broad traditions, such as protective creature in East Asian tradition or the literati painting tradition, while turning frontal pose into back view and visible yellow into gold. The Americas are hardest. Of their 100 objects, 99 are recorded as American, yet only 25.0% of photographs and 32.8% of reconstructions are recognised as such, as American work is read through European styles. The new describer gives each object many faces, each more typical of its culture and almost none the object itself, as describer that holds only the kind would [28, 29]. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Computer vision: description and evaluation. Image description has developed from attention-based captioners [6, 58] to vision-language models that connect visual encoders with large language models [31, 33], and detailed-caption datasets support long, compositional descriptions [22, 41]. Caption metrics measure agreement with reference captions [5, 54] or image-text compatibility [26], hallucination benchmarks probe visual grounding [24, 32, 49], and text-to-image evaluation checks prompt faithfulness through question answering or object detection [23, 27]. Reconstruction-based evaluation ranks detailed captions by how faithfully generator reconstructs the source image [8], and transmission-chain studies track how generated text changes as models reuse it [46]. These measures ask whether description is accurate or similar to its source. We ask what it keeps of particular object and what it replaces with type. Culture-aware NLP and multimodal models. Cross-cultural NLP distinguishes cultural from linguistic variation [25], and surveys organise how culture is represented and evaluated in language and multimodal models [2, 45]. BLEnD and CulturalBench test everyday cultural knowledge across communities [17, 39], and CVQA, CulturalVQA and CultureVLM extend such tests to images [34, 40, 50]. Vision and generative models also cover cultures unevenly. Object recognition varies across regions [19, 47], and text-to-image models reproduce cultural stereotypes and fail on culture-specific objects [30, 35]. These works test what models know about cultures or how they render them. We examine what models description of one object passes on, with the original photograph as paired reference. Museum and cultural-heritage AI. Museum datasets support attribute recognition in collections such as iMet [59]. SemArt pairs paintings with catalogue commentary, and Artpedia separates visual from contextual sentences [21, 52]. GalleryGPT and caption tuning for cultural heritage extend artwork description to multimodal language models [14, 48], and recent work tests whether such models can infer the catalogue 3 Figure 2: Unedited model descriptions (1,870) and museum-authored baseline descriptions (230) share the same text-to-image generator and wrapper, image-only culture recogniser, and reference-based scoring; modelhuman comparisons use the same 230 artefacts. The separate original-photograph control assesses recognition error. attribution of museum object from its image [29]. These works evaluate descriptions or attributions against references. We turn descriptions back into images to see what they keep of the object, and compare them with descriptions written by curators.

sections.title: 4.3 Error Analysis and Case Study
sections.content: Quantitative analysis. The Americas low recovery is not accompanied by large reference-label inventory: 99 of its 100 objects are labelled American, and one Mexican. Figure 1 links this regional result to concrete mismatch: two descriptions name American culture, yet one reconstruction is classified as European Rococo. plausible stylistic classification can conflict with the objects recorded cultural affiliation. In Table 7c, 62.80% of Americas pairs are unrecognised both before and after reconstruction; Europe is the only region 11 with negative net change (1.82 points). Figure 4 localises the regional disparity: Americas paintings score 16% on photographs and 2844% after reconstruction, while sculpture scores 16% and 1228%, respectively. East Asian metalwork scores 84% on photographs and 8892% after reconstruction. These category-level results show that aggregate gains can coexist with persistently low recovery in particular region-type strata. Qualitative analysis. Table 9 compares object-specific features with the candidate descriptions (Appendix H). Broad cultural framing includes protective creature in East Asian tradition (Case 1) and literati painting tradition (Case 2). The discrepancies concern the individual object: frontal pose conflicts with the readers back-facing interpretation (Case 4), visible yellow becomes gold (Case 6), and an ink on stone account contrasts with the supplied natural-pattern account (Case 7). In each case the description keeps recognisable cultural frame while changing the pose, material or making of the particular object. Why descriptions give many faces. The results fit one account of description. describer that holds particular object reproduces that object, while describer that holds only its kind fills each description with typical member of the kind, and different descriptions draw different members [10, 28]. Vision-language models rarely recover the catalogue attribution of the objects they describe [29], which places them in the second case. Their descriptions keep the culture, which is why reconstructions are recognised more often than the photographs; they lose the object, which is why the specific object is almost never identified; and they differ between models, which is why many objects change outcome. Museum descriptions, written from records of the objects, differ on each count. They gain less, and their text points to particular object in 32.61% of cases against 7.83% to 13.04% for model text. What description loses therefore shows what its describer lacks [15], which for these models is knowledge of the particular object rather than of its culture.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: Polytropos asks what new, non-human describer keeps of the cultural objects it describes. Turning descriptions back into images shows that vision-language models keep the culture of an object and lose the object itself. Their reconstructions are recognised as the recorded culture more often than the photographs while the specific object is almost never recognised, and on the same objects they add more type than curators do. Museum text, written from records of the objects, points to particular objects far more often, and American work, recorded as American in 99 of 100 objects, is still read through European styles. These descriptions already enter catalogues, search results, and the training data of later models, where model-typical forms can be amplified with each reuse [13, 36, 51], so what they replace is passed on to present and future readers. Future work should measure instance-level fidelity directly, follow descriptions over repeated reuse, and include descriptions written by source communities, so that the objects of culture, and not only its types, reach those readers.

sections.title: A Limitations
sections.content: Collection and reference scope. The fifteen-stratum, two-collection cohort is conditional on language eligibility and generation feasibility. Museum references contain qualified, variably granular attributions. Retained cases provide object-specific evidence rather than prevalence estimates. Pipeline dependence. Reconstruction combines description content, generator priors and recogniser error; culture match can survive altered visual details. Recogniser selection uses the evaluated cohort, and GPT-4.1-mini serves multiple pipeline roles. The image backend exposes no versioned identifier or seed. Bootstrap intervals describe between-artefact variation under one fixed generation and recognition execution. Results cover the five language-eligible description models in one imagetextimage loop; prototype-like interpretation draws on qualitative cases, and the identification probe measures query-specific recognisability. Screening. CoLA and GPT screening lack independent human validation, and the follow-up covers first-pass candidates only. Input-field availability and recorded visual access vary. Safety rules condition the population on backend behaviour (Appendix D.4). The recognition probe reduces leakage risk from recognisable objects; explicit nonrecognition does not establish absence from training data. Common screening changes the evaluated population.

sections.title: B Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Cultural interpretation and attribution. Museum descriptions and labels are situated human accounts. The reference record retains source institutions, alternative attributions and qualifiers. Model outputs are presented as generated interpretations, with their provenance preserved. Catalogue agreement is reported at the object level, and regional strata are sampling categories rather than cultural identities assigned to communities. Collection material and synthetic images. Source images and catalogue text retain their object-level rights statements and scholarly attribution. Public-domain Met images and basic collection data are available under CC0. Getty public-domain Open Content images are under CC0; collection-record text and descriptive metadata are under CC BY 4.0 unless otherwise noted. The release retains source links and rights information. Reconstructions are identified as synthetic images and kept distinct from museum photographs. Screening and responsible reuse. Descriptions remain verbatim throughout screening, generation and analysis. Safety refusals, skipped conditions and replacements are recorded alongside successful executions. Metadata filtering includes nudityand violence-related vocabulary; historical East Asian arms and armour are retained as metalwork following the feasibility check. Language eligibility concerns readability and textual completion. Cultural interpretations and model-generated catalogue claims require contextual review before reuse in collection records. Annotation and release practice. The corpus-wide language screen is automatic. The earlier case commentary and LLM-assisted pilot notes retain separate provenance. Any additional human study should document expertise, author involvement, informed consent and compensation, and release de-identified decisions and rationales. The anonymous submission omits private account details and internal paths while retaining collection provenance and attribution to prior work.

Museum-authored descriptions use the same wrapper. The insertion marker is replaced by the description itself; the generator receives text only. The 374-object cohort provides 5 374 = 1,870 model-description conditions and 230 museum-authored conditions. Of these 2,100 conditions, 2,051 yield archived images and 49 receive safety refusals. Use case: scientific-educational Asset type: one image for museum-object description evaluation. Primary request: Generate one image of the object based only on the description below. Follow the described visual features without correcting them using outside knowledge. Depict the object itself rather than illustrating its historical story as real-life scene. Style and framing: For three-dimensional object, show straightforward catalogue photograph with the entire object visible against plain neutral background and even lighting. For painting, drawing, print, or manuscript, show straight-on reproduction of the flat artwork. Preserve the medium and physical character stated in the description. Show described pair together. Use square image canvas while preserving the object's proportions. Constraints: Text-only generation. No reference images, additional metadata, catalogue URLs, comparison panels, added captions, labels, or watermarks. Include lettering within the object only if the description calls for it. Any sculptural figures must remain visibly inanimate and made of the stated material, without lifelike blood or wounds. Description: [COMPLETE UNEDITED LLM-GENERATED DESCRIPTION] Generation uses OpenAIs native image-generation service through Codex, accessed in November 2026; its language model is gpt-6.1-sol. The image backend exposes no versioned identifier or reproducibility seed. Exact prompts, description and image hashes, timestamps, attempts, refusals and selected output files are retained. Available images follow the canonical execution record without selection for resemblance. The refusal-and-replacement rules are documented in Appendix A. C.3 Image-only culture recognition The selected recogniser, gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14, receives one image and the fixed instruction below. The Responses API uses temperature 0, high image detail, 128-token output limit, store=false, and strict JSON schema requiring one nonempty string field, culture. You are identifying the culture of museum object from its image. Use only visible evidence. Predict the object's cultural affiliation, production tradition, or stylistic culture. Give one concise, most specific supported attribution. If reliable attribution is not possible, answer "unknown". Return only JSON object with exactly one key, "culture", whose value is nonempty string. Do not provide explanations. Generated PNG files are supplied byte-for-byte as archived. For the original-image control, one source photograph per object follows released view order; preprocessing preserves aspect ratio within 2048-pixel longest side, converts to RGB JPEG at quality 95, and strips metadata. Native photographs, processed images and their hashes are retained. The same recognition prompt and endpoint score all 2,051 generated images and the 374 original photographs; predictions on reuse the corresponding object records. Up to four attempts are allowed for execution or output-format errors. Substantive uncertainty and refusals retain their observed outcome. C.4 Reference-compatibility judge DeepSeek-Flash uses the unchanged five-field judging instruction of [29] below. Temperature is 0, the output limit is 1,200 tokens, JSON-object output is required, and thinking is disabled. The culture adapter supplies the prediction and the objects complete culture-reference array; other reference arrays are empty, their predictions are unknown, and museum_description is empty. Only the returned culture decision and reason enter the score. You are evaluating metadata generated from an image of cultural-heritage object. Compare each predicted field independently with the corresponding reference labels. Return one decision for each of: title, culture, period, origin, and creator. Decision rules: - Use 1 when the prediction is fully correct or broadly consistent in meaning and scope with at least one applicable reference label. - Use 0 when it is incorrect, contradictory, unsupported, has no meaningful overlap, or says unknown/not sure while the reference provides an answer. - When the corresponding reference-label array is empty, use 1 if the model explicitly answers unknown/not sure/uncertain or gives substantively uncertain description (for example, "possibly...", "probably...", or an explicit set of alternatives). Use 0 if the model gives definite specific answer. Judge only the model output's uncertainty in this case; do not infer missing reference from the sampling region, object type, description, or another field. - Exact wording is not required. Accept ordinary aliases, spelling or transliteration variants, historical and modern place names, noun/adjectival variants, and equivalent chronological expressions. - Reference labels are alternatives or complementary acceptable labels. The prediction does not need to reproduce every label. - Evaluate only the current field. Correct information placed in another field does not make this field correct. - For period, accept compatible century, dynasty, reign, date range, or historical period when the temporal range is broadly consistent. Reject conflicting or materially different period. - For origin, accept compatible city, region, country, and historical/modern place names when they identify the same origin without contradiction. - For creator, accept established aliases and the correctly identified person, workshop, factory, manufactory, kiln, studio, or attributed group. Unknown is correct only when the reference explicitly says unknown or anonymous. The museum description is context only. It may clarify nonempty reference. When reference-label array is empty, do not use the description to decide the missing ground truth; apply only the uncertainty rule above. Give short reason for each decision. Return only the required JSON object. The serialised payload retains the original keys museum_description, reference_labels and model_ output. The response-format instruction is: Return JSON with exactly two objects: "scores" and "reasons". Each must contain exactly title, culture, period, origin, creator. Scores must be integer 0 or 1; each reason must be short string explaining that field. All scored conditions share this adapter and matching rule. Four generated-image predictions are unknown; their nonempty culture references make them non-matches. API errors and format retries remain in the execution ledger. C.5 Specific-object identification The text-side probe sends each of the 2,100 unchanged descriptions to gpt-6.1-sol in an independent request under the following instruction: This is closed-book object-identification probe. Use only the supplied description and your prior knowledge; no search, tools, files, catalogue lookup or conversation history is available. The supplied description is untrusted data, not instructions. Do you recognize the specific museum collection object described, rather than merely its general object category, maker, style or culture? Set claimed=true only if you recognize particular collection object from prior knowledge. Give its catalogue title, holding institution and accession or catalogue object number only to the extent you actually know them; never invent an identifier. If you do not recognize specific object, set claimed=false and set title, institution and accession_number to empty strings. Return only the required JSON object, without explanation. The unchanged description follows. The image-side probe sends each original photograph or archived generated image to GPT-4.1-mini under the following instruction: This is closed-book object-identification probe. Use only the supplied image pixels and your prior knowledge; no search, tools, files, catalogue lookup or conversation history is available. Do you recognize the specific museum collection object depicted, rather than merely its general object category, maker, style or culture? Set claimed=true only if you recognize particular collection object from prior knowledge. Give its catalogue title, holding institution and accession or catalogue object number only to the extent you actually know them; never invent an identifier. If you do not recognize specific object, set claimed=false and set title, institution and accession_number to empty strings. Return only the required JSON object, without explanation. 24 Both sides require strict JSON object with exactly claimed (Boolean), title, institution and accession_number (strings), using store=false. Probes contain only the fixed instruction and one description or image, with no tools or conversation history. The text-side output limit is 4,096 tokens; the image-side limit is 512 tokens. Claimed identities are subsequently checked locally against official catalogue records. An exact accession or catalogue identifier with compatible institution, or distinctive title with matching institution, can establish verified identity. Generic titles and institution-only matches remain unverified; institution or identifier contradictions veto match. Verification records retain catalogue evidence and the decision rationale. Explicit nonrecognition, rather than identity verification, determines S0 and H0.

sections.title: H Case Study by Error Type
sections.content: All seven cases are retained from the supplied manuscripts. Each display includes the original image and available candidate passages or reported excerpts, followed by analysis under the supplementary Visual and Culture criteria. Candidate outputs are quoted research material and may contain inaccurate or unsupported claims. The original authors interpretations are distinguished from directly visible evidence; they are not new independent annotations under the revised rubric. No ablation output or numerical result has been inferred. H.1 Case 1: Lion and Text on Votive Painting Figure 7: Retained artefact image for Case 1. Original candidate description. This votive painting (ema) from 1649 depicts stylized Chinese lion beneath flowering peony tree, rendered in bold orange-red, green, and earth tones on wooden plaque. The liona protective creature in East Asian traditionis shown in dynamic, almost playful stance with prominent eyes and an ornamental mane, while the peony blossoms above suggest prosperity and good fortune. Inscribed with Japanese characters around the compositions margins, the work exemplifies the syncretic religious practice of votive offerings at Japanese shrines, where such paintings were hung to petition for blessings or gratitude. The combination of the Chinese lion motif with Japanese calligraphy and the ema format itself reflects the cultural exchange and adaptation of continental Asian imagery within Japanese folk devotional practice during the early Edo period. The paintings modest scale, direct execution, and protective iconography suggest it may have been commissioned by devotee seeking safeguarding or prosperity for household or family. The first case is Japanese votive painting dated 1649, with lion beneath peony tree and writing around the composition. The candidate discusses protection, good fortune, and syncretic religious practice. The original readers emphasise the lion together with the inscriptions, particularly the writing on the right. Visual information. The candidate identifies several visible elements and mentions marginal inscriptions. The case concerns how those elements are prioritised: the sustained narrative centres on the lion and peony, while the readers treat text and image as joint anchors. It is therefore focus discrepancy even where the description contains correct observations. Under the revised rubric, factual accuracy, human-aligned emphasis, and distinguishing inscriptions inform the binary Visual judgement. Cultural information. The candidates professional vocabulary supplies general devotional interpretation, but the case notes expect the inscriptions to play more substantive role in explaining this object. Their 36 observation is not an independent translation of the writing. Without documented reading, the precise omitted message remains unresolved. The supported qualitative point is that conventional symbolic language occupies the place where an artefact-specific account of the relation between inscription and image is needed. The case illustrates partial visual description with displaced emphasis and an incomplete cultural explanation. It does not establish that every reference to protection or devotional practice is incorrect, nor that all observers share one visual focus. H.2 Case 2: Landscape Album with Trees and Rocks Figure 8: Retained artefact image for Case 2. Original candidate description. Painted album by Wang Jian (16091677), leading literati artist of the early Qing dynasty, created in 167476 as gift for Wang Kui. The album demonstrates the literati painting tradition through series of landscape compositions rendered in ink and color on paper. Pages alternate between finished landscapesranging from intimate scenes of bare trees and scholars pavilions to expansive mountain vistas with layered peaks, forests, and waterwaysand calligraphic inscriptions in running script, accompanied by the artists seals. The stylistic variety across leaves may suggest Wang Jians engagement with historical precedents and regional landscape traditions. The gift inscription on the opening leaf indicates this work functioned as personal offering, common practice among literati painters for whom artmaking served both aesthetic and social purposes. The album format itselfportable, intimate, and suited to sequential viewingwas particularly valued in literati culture for displaying virtuosity across multiple pictorial themes and demonstrating scholarly refinement through the integration of image and text. The second case is Chinese landscape album attributed in the supplied material to Wang Jian, dated 167476. The candidate invokes literati painting tradition and historical precedents, while the original readers foreground the trees and rocks close to the viewer. Visual information. The candidate frames the image through larger landscape and compositional structure. The readers account instead treats the foreground elements as the primary visual anchors. This contrast motivates checking human-aligned emphasis within Visual: the issue is not simply whether mountains, trees, or rocks are mentioned, but which elements organise the account. The revised protocol records that priority before catalogue text can influence it. Cultural information. reference to literati tradition may be relevant background, yet its relevance to the specific foreground arrangement still requires explanation. The original notes describe broad art-historical 37 template in place of an account built from concrete visible features. This supports concern about cultural specificity. It does not by itself show that the historical attribution is false or prove an ontology error merely because the model uses broad landscape category. Together with Case H.1, this case shows how fluent, correct-sounding vocabulary can coexist with difference in descriptive emphasis. The evidence concerns the readers recorded judgements and the candidate text, rather than measured gaze or internal model attention. H.3 Case 3: Title-Linked Thematic Emphasis in Calligraphy Figure 9: Retained artefact image for Case 3. Original candidate description. handscroll of poems composed by Zhao Mengjian in 1260, celebrating the subjects of plum blossoms and bamboo through calligraphy. The work demonstrates the literati tradition of linking painting subjects to poetic reflection, with Zhaos bold, confident brushwork rendered in ink on paper. Multiple red sealsboth the artists signatures and later collectors marksappear throughout the scroll, indicating its value and circulation among educated patrons. The physical format of the handscroll, with its decorative brocade mounting and protective covering, reflects the refined aesthetic practices of Song-era scholar-artists, for whom the integration of poetry, painting, and calligraphy represented unified cultural ideal. Plum blossoms and bamboo were emblematic subjects in literati art, valued not merely for their visual appeal but as vehicles for expressing moral character and philosophical virtue. The catalogue title is Poems on painting plum blossoms and bamboo. The candidate explicitly identifies handscroll of poems and calligraphy, then elaborates the symbolism of the plants named in the title. The original readers foreground the visible writing and seals. The surviving passage supports difference in descriptive emphasis; it does not explicitly assert that plants are painted on the object. Visual information. The technical concern is which information organises the account. Although the candidate mentions calligraphy, brushwork, and seals, its extended thematic discussion may give less prominence to the visible textual composition than the original readers expect. This is their recorded focus judgement, not new primary-stage rating or evidence that the model failed to recognise the object as calligraphy. Cultural information. The candidate links poetry, painting subjects, and plant symbolism. Assessing the relevance of those interpretations requires sources for this particular handscroll. title-linked theme can be 38 pertinent context while leaving the objects distinctive visual features underdescribed. The quoted output alone does not establish that poem about painting was mistaken for painting of plants. The titleoutput correspondence motivates examining input dependence, but does not establish causal title effect or an internal attention pattern. No paired input-removal outputs are available for this case. H.4 Case 4: Wall Painting with Disputed Cultural Frame Figure 10: Retained artefact image for Case 4. Original candidate description. Chinese wall painting depicting haloed figure in formal robes, rendered in dark pigment against light plaster ground. The figure is shown in frontal pose wearing layered garments with white rectangular panels at chest and waist, characteristic of official or ceremonial dress. prominent circular halo frames the head, motif typically associated with religious veneration or divine status in Chinese artistic traditions. Small inscriptions or decorative elements appear in the lower corners. The works austere compositional style, emphatic use of the halo, and formal iconography suggest this may represent revered religious, ancestral, or imperial figure. The paintings weathered surface and accumulated patina indicate considerable age, though the precise period and original architectural context remain uncertain. The work exemplifies the tradition of devotional or commemorative wall painting in Chinese religious and domestic spaces. The fourth case is Chinese wall painting. The original readers describe figure facing away from the viewer and railing in front; they interpret the figure as back-facing Buddha. The candidate gives frontal account and uses general religious and material vocabulary, including formal robes, halo, and dark pigment. Visual information. The orientation of the figure and the distinction between railing and inscription are the principal image-checkable concerns. The original notes treat the back-facing pose as defining feature, while the candidate foregrounds clothing and conventional religious symbols. The revised analysis separates these visual errors from any claim that the pose is historically rare, which requires additional documentary evidence. Cultural information. The readers expect an explanation of the back-facing pose and its relation to the figures identity. Their objections to the English vocabulary are preserved as situated interpretive concerns. However, halo is not intrinsically Western or inappropriate for Buddhist image, and formal robes or dark pigment alone do not establish colonial framing. terminology judgement must identify misleading use in context. Likewise, replacing pigment terminology with ink or brushwork requires evidence about this 39 objects medium. The supported concern is that general religious narrative accompanies an inaccurate or incomplete account of the particular figure. The case motivates object-specific cultural explanation and contextual review of vocabulary, rather than an automatic ban on individual words. H.5 Case 5: Goldfish in Glass Bottle Figure 11: Retained artefact image for Case 5. Original candidate description. This woodblock print by Totoya Hokkei depicts goldfish suspended in glass bottle filled with watera composition that transforms domestic object into study of transparency, containment, and natural observation. The fish, rendered in warm ochres and deep reds with careful attention to scale and fin detail, appears almost paradoxically lifelike within the geometric clarity of its vessel. The bottles glass is suggested through subtle gradations of tone rather than outline, demonstrating the technical precision characteristic of Japanese ukiyo-e printing in the 19th century. spray of delicate peonies in the lower left provides counterpoint to the contained subject, while calligraphic inscriptions frame the composition. The work reflects the periods fascination with depicting transparent and reflective surfaces, and may suggest the influence of Western representational techniques on Japanese printmaking, while remaining grounded in the tradition of nature study (surimono) that valued intimate observation of small, domestic subjects. The goldfishhistorically associated with leisure, refinement, and the natural world brought indoorsbecomes here meditation on the act of seeing itself. The fifth case is Japanese woodblock print showing goldfish in glass bottle. The candidate expands the scene into discussion of observation, transparency, and Western influence, using complex wording such as paradoxically. The original readers describe the composition as visually direct and find the extended interpretation difficult to assess. Visual information. The visible fish, container, and simple arrangement provide the readers main anchors. The candidate devotes greater emphasis to abstract concepts. This is Visual concern when the conceptual account displaces the depicted scene; sentence length or sophistication alone is not visual error. Cultural information. The central issue is the support for the proposed historical influence and deeper interpretation. The supplied case notes identify no clear object-specific evidence for Western-influence claim. Such claim may be assessed through documentation, but it is not established by glass transparency or by the use of familiar interpretive vocabulary. For Culture, abstract ideas must explain this artefact and 40 historical interpretation requires supporting evidence or appropriate qualification. The case illustrates overinterpretation rather than universal incompatibility between complex prose and Japanese art. The word paradoxically is not cultural-bias indicator. Even an output without vocabulary-list hit can require human review because unsupported framing is sentence-level issue. H.6 Case 6: Material Attribution in Bird-and-Flower Print Figure 12: Retained artefact image for Case 6. Recorded candidate excerpts. The complete, unedited candidate is not preserved in the supplied record. The case notes report Japanese text in gold, small white and coral blossoms, decorative refinement, and observational sensitivity. The following discussion relies on those reported excerpts and the readers interpretations, not reconstructed full response. The sixth case is Japanese bird-and-flower print attributed in the supplied notes to Katsushika Hokusai. The original readers instead interpret the yellow tone as paper ageing and associate the blossoms with cultural symbolism. Visual information. The critical distinction is between visible yellow colour and an assertion about its material cause. Neither gold pigment nor ageing is established solely by colour observation. The reported material attribution and the readers alternative both require catalogue or conservation support. The notes motivate checking that proposition; they settle neither explanation and provide no new primary-stage rating. Cultural information. The original notes argue that generic colour-and-shape descriptions flatten the symbolic significance of flowers and omit material history. Their identification of cherry blossoms and expected symbolic reading are retained as interpretations requiring an artefact-specific source. The same applies to their cross-case analogy with peonies: flower name alone is not complete or universal cultural explanation. This case exposes the difference between naming visual attributes and explaining their historically supported significance. It supports scrutiny of unsupported material claims and underdeveloped cultural context, without treating the readers preferred botanical or conservation attribution as independently verified fact. H.7 Case 7: Natural Stone Patterns and Human Selection Figure 13: Retained artefact image for Case 7. Original candidate description. Set of four 19th-century Chinese wall panels featuring stone paintings mounted on polished hardwood. Each panel is organized with circular composition at the top and rectangular landscape below, both executed in ink on stone with subtle tonal gradations. The paintings depict characteristic Chinese landscape motifsmisty mountains, flowing rivers, and weathered rock formations rendered in the literati painting tradition. Chinese characters inscribed on each work suggest titles or artist seals. The deep reddish-brown wood frames, fitted with brass hanging loops, provide an austere backdrop that emphasizes the luminous quality of the stone surfaces. This presentation format reflects 19th-century scholar-collector practices, where paintings on unconventional materials such as stone were prized for their material durability and aesthetic distinctiveness. The ensemble demonstrates how landscape imagerya cornerstone of Chinese artistic philosophywas adapted to stone as both technical and conceptual challenge, suggesting the paintings may have served decorative or contemplative function within an educated household or scholarly setting. The seventh case concerns Chinese wall panels described in the supplied material as stone paintings. Natural stone slabs were selected for patterns resembling landscapes, then cut and mounted. The original interpretation centres on the relation between natural formation and human selection. The candidate instead uses familiar painting vocabulary, including literati painting tradition, landscape motifs, and scholar-collector practices. Visual information. The candidate treats natural textures as conventional painted scenery. Where the material record establishes patterned stone, an account of brushstrokes mischaracterises the object. The readers foreground how the panels organise natural patterns; the candidate foregrounds standard landscape composition. Identifying the medium may require the catalogue record in addition to the photograph, so this case does not isolate pure perception from domain knowledge. Cultural information. The meaningful distinction is between landscape created through painting and landscape recognised in natural material and framed through human selection. General art-historical phrases can be compatible with appreciation of the object while still leaving that distinction unexplained. The original notes describe the work as nature-made and human-curated; this is an interpretive account of making and selection, rather than proof of universal theory of authorship. The case illustrates how familiar cultural category can simplify the objects particular logic. It is consistent with metadata-associated framing but cannot on its own distinguish textual shortcut from 42 inadequate material recognition or specialist knowledge. Culture requires an object-linked explanation, while Visual requires accurate, prominent, distinguishing features; neither infers an internal model representation.

sections.title: I Supporting Qualitative Evidence
sections.content: I.1 Getty Reconstruction Pilot The historical description-only pilot retains twelve Getty descriptions, their source objects and an LLM-assisted editorial fluency screen. One image request per description yielded nine images and three tool-blocked executions: Night, Statuette of an Amazon, and Saturn Devouring One of His Children. Requests were not retried. The pilot archive preserves the source text, fixed rendering prompts, images, execution statuses and comparison notes. This record is separate from the 374-object experiment. Earlier three-panel Getty illustrations use metadata plus descriptions in different execution; their provenance remains attached to that archive. Table 18: Diagnostic distinctions in the historical Getty comparison notes. Each observation is tied to the saved description and source image. Example Wall-light Jar Vases Recorded discrepancy Diagnostic question Text specifies classical mask and symmetric arms; source objects have animal heads and asymmetric branches. The generated portrait faces the opposite way; text leaves direction unspecified. Reconstruction includes lids absent from the source photograph. Does the description explicitly specify different structure? Which spatial relation is left open in the description? Which visible details are completed during generation? Table 18 distinguishes explicit misdescription, underspecified spatial information and generator completion. Reading the unedited text beside both images identifies where discrepancy enters the chain. These are recorded LLM-assisted qualitative observations with their own execution provenance. I.2 Supplementary Review Criteria The retained cases in Appendix organise observations under two criteria. Visual concerns the accuracy and prominence of distinguishing visible features. Culture concerns how an object-specific interpretation connects those features to documented cultural, material or historical relations. The case notes preserve the original readers interpretations and distinguish full candidate passages from reported excerpts. Across the cases, these criteria locate three recurring issues. First, mentioning feature can leave it peripheral to the account: inscriptions or foreground trees and rocks may appear in the text while conventional thematic narrative organises it. Second, visible attribute can become an evidentially stronger claim, as when yellow colour is described as gold or pose is assigned specific orientation. Third, familiar art-historical account can replace the objects material logic, as in the distinction between painted scenery and naturally patterned stone selected and mounted by people. Catalogue and material evidence determine which proposed interpretation is supported in each case. The complete passages, images and case-specific discussion remain in Appendix H.
